notes.meaning: Israel arrived at the desert around Mount Sinai about seven weeks after leaving Egypt. This timing points forward to the Feast of Pentecost, which was later celebrated fifty days after Passover. God led them through the wilderness to the very mountain where He first spoke to Moses.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars note that the word translated 'wilderness' means uncultivated grazing land suitable for flocks, rather than a sandy desert.

notes.meaning: The Israelites broke camp at Rephidim and pitched their tents directly in front of Mount Sinai. This fulfilled God's earlier promise that Moses and the people would return to worship Him at this exact mountain. The wide valley gave the massive community ample room to camp together before God.

Moses climbed the mountain to seek God in quiet prayer away from the camp. The Lord called out to him from the heights and gave him a message for the whole nation. Calling them both the 'house of Jacob' and the 'sons of Israel' reminded them of their humble beginnings and how God had grown them into a nation.

God reminded the people of how He judged the Egyptians and rescued Israel with great power. He compared His care to an eagle carrying its young safely on its wings above danger. Most of all, God brought them out of slavery so they could enjoy close fellowship with Himself.

God offered Israel a covenant, which is a binding agreement of relationship and loyalty. If they listened to His voice and kept His commands, they would be His prized treasure above all other peoples. Even though the entire earth belongs to the Lord, He chose them for a special purpose.

The Lord promised that Israel would be a kingdom of priests, meaning a community where all the people had access to worship and serve Him. They were also to be a holy nation, set apart from the wicked ways of the world to reflect God's pure character. Christians later receive this same royal and priestly calling through faith in Christ.

Moses came down the mountain and gathered the elders, who were the respected leaders of each tribe. He shared with them every word the Lord had commanded without leaving anything out. By setting God's words before them, Moses gave the people an honest choice to accept God's covenant.

The people answered with one voice, promising to do everything the Lord had commanded. Though their willingness was sincere, they spoke with overconfidence and did not realize how weak their hearts truly were. Moses then carried their answer back to God, acting as a mediator who represented the people before the Lord.

God told Moses that He would appear in a dense, dark cloud so the people could actually hear Him speaking with Moses. Hearing God's voice would remove all doubts and teach the people to trust Moses as God's true prophet for generations to come. The dark cloud also veiled God's brilliant glory so that sinful human eyes were not overwhelmed.

The Lord told Moses to consecrate the people over the next two days, which meant setting them apart for sacred worship. They were ordered to wash their clothes as an outward symbol of turning away from sin. This reminded the people that anyone who approaches the holy God must seek inner purity and clean hearts.

The people were told to finish their preparations by the third day, when the Lord would descend upon Mount Sinai before the whole camp. Taking two full days to prepare showed that approaching God is a serious matter that cannot be rushed. God wanted every person to await His arrival with deep respect and eager attention.

Moses was commanded to set up a boundary around the base of the mountain to keep the people at a distance. Anyone who stepped over the line or touched the mountain was to be put to death immediately. This strict rule taught Israel that God is holy and separate from sinful human beings.

If a person or animal touched the mountain, no one was allowed to run past the boundary to seize them. Instead, the trespasser had to be put to death from a distance with stones or arrows so others would not become defiled. Only when the long horn blast sounded were the appointed leaders permitted to come near.

Moses went down from the mountain and led the people in their time of consecration. The people washed their clothes and put aside their daily work to prepare for the Lord's arrival. Their obedience showed that they took God's instructions to heart.

Moses warned the people to be fully ready for the third day and told husbands and wives to abstain from physical intimacy. This temporary restraint did not mean marriage was sinful, but it helped them set aside ordinary desires to focus completely on God. God desired their wholehearted devotion during this solemn encounter.

On the morning of the third day, fierce lightning flashed, thunder crashed, and a thick cloud covered the mountain. A supernatural trumpet blasted with a sound so loud and piercing that everyone in the camp trembled with dread. These terrifying signs reminded the people of the supreme power and majesty of God.

Moses led the trembling people out of their camp to stand near the foot of the mountain outside the boundary. Even though the display was terrifying, God had gathered them to meet with Him and hear His word. Standing before the mountain reminded them that true worship includes reverent awe.

Mount Sinai was wrapped in heavy smoke because the Lord came down upon it in fire. The smoke rose like the smoke of a giant furnace, and the entire mountain shook violently in a great earthquake. These visible wonders showed that the holy God is like a consuming fire to all sin.

As the sound of the ram's horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke to the Lord. God answered him aloud in a voice that thundered across the mountain. This public conversation proved to the whole assembly that Moses was God's chosen prophet who spoke with divine authority.

The Lord came down upon the very summit of Mount Sinai and called Moses to come up. Moses obeyed and climbed up the mountain, demonstrating remarkable courage and faith amid the smoke and trembling rock. He could approach the fiery summit only because God had personally invited him.

The Lord immediately ordered Moses to go back down and warn the people against breaking through the barrier. God knew that people might be tempted by curiosity to push forward and gaze at His glory. If they rushed past the boundary, many would perish, because sinful mortals cannot gaze upon the unshielded presence of God.

God gave a special warning that the priests must also purify themselves before coming near. These priests were tribal and family leaders who offered sacrifices before the family of Aaron was formally set apart. No sacred title or religious role excused anyone from God's strict requirements for holiness.

Moses replied to the Lord that the people would not come up because the boundary had already been set and the warning given. He assumed that the physical barriers and initial commands were enough to keep everyone in line. Moses thought the people were reliable, but God knew the hidden weakness and curiosity of the human heart.

The Lord dismissed Moses' objection and commanded him to go down immediately and bring Aaron back up with him. He repeated that neither the priests nor the rest of the people were permitted to force their way past the boundary. God repeated this command out of mercy, protecting the people from the fatal consequences of their own rashness.

Moses set aside his own thoughts, went down to the camp, and delivered the Lord's warning to the people. He reminded them to stay behind the barriers and treat God's holy presence with deep reverence. His prompt obedience helped keep the nation safe as they prepared to hear the Ten Commandments.
